chapter: Road shows in the Southwest and Midwest
title: Structure of a minstrel show and the Spikes Brothers' instruments
summary: Spikes explains the minstrel first part, the olio and the finale, and the xylophone, chimes, ragtime and saxophone numbers in their act.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Can I go back a ways? Tell me, when you and your brother first had the duo in Arizona, what kind of music were you
playing then? What were the...do you remember specifically any of the tunes that were popular then or the kinds of music you were playing?
Well, we had a regular minstrel opening. You know what a minstrel opening is?
No, I don't, but I'd like to find out.

You have a opening song, and then everybody sits in a circle, the comedians on the end tell the jokes, and the interlocutor talks to the comedian, and he cracks his joke, and then you introduce the singer, and she sings. Then you go into the next joke and the next dancer and so forth, see? And that's a minstrel opening. And then you have what you call an olio. After that, you have a little act of some kind. And then if you got like we were, the center of attraction, we do our musical act in what you call the olio. Then the next guy maybe had a dog act where he could walk on his hind legs and jump over a hoop and all like that or juggle some ...uh, you know what I'm talking about--the balls shaped like a beer bottle--what do you call them things?
Oh, yeah, like the bowling pin thing?

Yeah, and they had a lot of acts those days-- acrobatic acts and juggling acts, you know. Course they're out of date now--all that stuff. Anyway, that's what you call the olio. Then you had a finale act, which was a big singing act and a dancing act and so forth. That closed the show. Nearly all of them had the same program, the same thing down, but they generally opened--nearly

all the colored shows nearly generally opened with the minstrel first part. You see? You'd have this group all sitting around, and you had the interlocutor. He was the man who introduced you, and he'd ...and like you'd say, "Well, Mr. Jones, what are you doing in there?" "Oh, I ain't doin' nuthin!' "Who's that woman I saw you with the other day?" "Well, that wasn't no woman. That was my wife." You know, jokes! Things like that. And "Why did the chicken cross the street?" "Well, I don't know, why?" "Because he wanted to get on the other side." You know. Those old jokes, you know, a hundred years old, that's what the interlocutor was for, you know, and he say, oh, you know, jokes like that, and that was the minstrel first part. Then you went into your olio which was from the first act to the last act, that was where your specialties all were, see? You'd do three or four specialties in there like vaudeville, and then you had your finale. That was the show. All of them practically done that way--even Georgia Minstrels and all of those big shows. It was the same routine mostly, you know, and that's the way that was.
How about the music? When you and your brother came along, what did you play?

We played our instruments. We didn't have The Musical Meat Market because we give that up. It was too much for this little show to travel. We just had the regular instruments-- like Lionel with his xylophone and things. Then we'd walk over and play the chimes, you know, the big chimes, some of them this big, you know, and I think we played "Miserere" from "Il Trovatore" and things
